headings: Plan the journey to your Conditional Access baseline.
summaries: What IAMAI asks for, and how to remove it
sentences: IAMAI reads a Microsoft Entra tenant, compares it with a published Conditional Access baseline, and writes a dated plan to close the gaps without locking anyone out.
It is read-only and runs in this browser.
The person doing security at a small MSP or a small business, on their own, who has to get this done in a few weeks.
An admin whose only sign-in method is a text message, about to be required to use a passkey.
An emergency access account inside the policy it exists to survive.
A country rule that blocks the person who wrote it.
A service account that a legacy-authentication block stops at 2 a.m.
A meeting-room device that a session rule signs out every hour.
Sign in with a Global Administrator or Global Reader account.
Entra ID P1 adds sign-in evidence; the plan works without it.

A published set of Conditional Access policies, built and maintained by Jon Hope, Microsoft MVP, at ConditionalAccess.Tech.
Its aim is layered protection for a small organisation: MFA for everyone, phishing-resistant admins, constrained sessions and devices, and emergency access that survives every policy.
IAMAI compares what each policy is for with what {tenant} has, and plans the difference.
About ten minutes.
Reads the tenant into this browser; nothing is sent anywhere.

surfaces.name: Plan / one step opened
headings: If a change locks you out
sentences: Create or Correct Emergency Access Accounts Ready
Done together with Create or Correct Exclusions Group: these accounts are the members of that group, and the group is what every policy excludes.
Emergency access accounts are how you keep access to Contoso Pty Ltd if a change goes wrong.
Learn →
The emergency access accounts, and every policy that must exclude them:
Break-glass 01
Your own account, Alex Morgan, is not one of these and must not be.
Tick every account that exists only for this purpose; two are needed.
IAMAI nominated these from their names, roles and exclusions.
Create the rest below.
Fix each failing check, top to bottom.
3 of 18 checks fail today.
Create a second account: one account is a single point of failure.
Break-glass 01: assign Global Administrator permanently and actively; an eligible role has to activate first, and activation is one of the things a bad policy can block.
Break-glass 01 looks like a person's account (it has department Operations); use a dedicated account instead.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → New user.
Name it so the purpose is obvious (Emergency Access).
Sign-in address on the tenant's own onmicrosoft.com domain; cloud-only; no licence; no department, title or manager.
Roles → assign Global Administrator, active and permanent.
Set a passphrase of at least 20 random characters.
Store it offline in two places that different people can reach without signing in to this tenant, for example a sealed envelope in a safe and a second copy with the business owner.
Never in a mailbox, a chat, or a password manager that needs this tenant to sign in.
Register a hardware security key (FIDO2) for each account and keep it with the passphrase.
Not a passkey in Authenticator: that lives on a person's phone.
Do not share a key between accounts.
All 18 checks pass on the next scan.
Both passphrases are stored offline in two places, and two named people know where.
Sign in with one of the emergency accounts above, in a private browser window.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Conditional Access → Policies → open the policy that changed today → Enable policy: Report-only (or Off) → Save.
It applies within minutes.

If the portal itself is blocked: sign in from a device and network the policies trust (a managed laptop on the office network), or from any device run Connect-MgGraph -Scopes Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess and then Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId <id> -State enabledForReportingButNotEnforced.
If no route works, Microsoft support can help; they will ask for the tenant id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000.

surfaces.name: How IAMAI works
links: Microsoft: plan a Conditional Access deployment
Microsoft: network assignment and named locations
Microsoft: Conditional Access for workload identities
sentences: Every check IAMAI runs, generated from the rules the code runs from.
What a package is, three ways to make one, and what IAMAI does with it.
Entra admin center
PowerShell (Microsoft Graph SDK)
Exports from other tools
IAMAI approximates how Microsoft evaluates a sign-in; report-only is the truth.
Some conditions, like device filters and token state, it cannot reproduce.
Without Entra ID P1 there is no impact analysis; the plan is licence, then security defaults, then Conditional Access.
Sign-in history shows behaviour under today's policy; it cannot see who would register MFA when first prompted.
There is no server: no scheduled re-scans, no alerts, no state shared across devices.
A sign-in session lasts about a day; the plan file never depends on it, so save the plan to keep it.
No AI runs in these tools.
Every plan is computed from the tenant's own records; the Export page writes prompts for your own assistant, not the other way round.
